The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch', intended to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), thereby emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This paradigmatic shift in geological thought (Barnosky et al., 2011) seeks to underscore the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence (Witze, 2024).

In this context, the Anthropocene epoch represents a critical juncture in the Earth's geological history, marking a profound departure from the Holocene epoch (Barnosky et al., 2011). The Anthropocene's designation acknowledges the far-reaching consequences of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems, including climate change, deforestation, and habitat destruction (Nixon, 2011). By recognizing the Anthropocene epoch, scientists and scholars aim to promote a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between human societies and the Earth's biophysical systems (Haraway, 2016).

Furthermore, the Anthropocene's introduction has sparked a broader discussion on the nature of geological time and the role of human activities in shaping the Earth's biophysical systems (Barnosky et al., 2011). This new paradigm challenges traditional notions of geological time and highlights the need for a more inclusive and dynamic understanding of the Earth's history (Smith & Zeder, 2013). Ultimately, the Anthropocene epoch serves as a powerful tool for promoting environmental awareness and encouraging sustainable practices, as it underscores the critical importance of mitigating the impacts of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024).
